{"externally_confirmed_facts":["`javax.net.ssl.SSLContext` represents a secure socket protocol implementation. It is initialized with key managers, trust managers, and a secure-random source, and it provides factories for `SSLSocketFactory`, `SSLServerSocketFactory`, and `SSLEngine` objects. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html","The reported finding refers to the `tm` value—the second argument—in `SSLContext.init(KeyManager[] km, TrustManager[] tm, SecureRandom random)`. The `SSLContext` API says that, when `tm` is non-null, the implementation uses the supplied trust-manager array (using only the first instance of a particular trust-manager implementation type). When `tm` is null, installed security providers are searched for a suitable `TrustManagerFactory` implementation. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html","Neither the API’s `init` signature nor its documented exceptions defines the detector phrases “application defines” or “was not observed coming from a TrustManagerFactory.” Those phrases describe provenance asserted by the detector. The cited CrySL rule does not contain those phrases and does not name `TrustManagerFactory`; it requires `generatedTrustManagers[tm]`. The rule file alone therefore does not establish the mapping between that predicate and the detector presentation text.","Official JSSE documentation permits trust managers obtained from a `TrustManagerFactory` and concrete application implementations. It states that trust managers can be created by a `TrustManagerFactory` or by providing a concrete implementation; an `X509TrustManager` can be implemented directly, obtained from a provider factory, or delegate to a factory-generated manager. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html","For an `X509TrustManager`, the documented trust-decision contract is to build a certification path to a trusted root and return only when that path can be validated and trusted for the applicable authentication type. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/X509TrustManager.html","The official `SSLContext` and JSSE sources do not state that an application-defined trust manager is categorically invalid, nor do they prescribe a mandatory replacement of every custom manager with a `TrustManagerFactory` result. Documented alternatives include: passing null for `tm` to use provider selection; using a `TrustManagerFactory` with a `KeyStore` or provider-specific parameters; or implementing/delegating an `X509TrustManager` where custom behavior is needed. Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManagerFactory.html ; https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html","Trust-path validation and endpoint identification are distinct documented controls. The JSSE reference guide identifies endpoint identification during the TLS handshake through `SSLParameters.setEndpointIdentificationAlgorithm` and says applications using raw `SSLSocket` or `SSLEngine` APIs should check peer credentials before sending data. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html","The reviewed `SSLContext`, `TrustManagerFactory`, and `X509TrustManager` API documentation defines in-memory interfaces and initialization behavior. It does not define a persisted format, serialization format, TLS wire-format migration, or a migration procedure specifically for changing the origin of the `TrustManager[]` passed to `SSLContext.init`. This is a limitation of the reviewed API documentation, not a claim that different trust-manager implementations have equivalent behavior.","Protocol selection is separate from trust-manager provenance. The Java standard-names documentation distinguishes SSLContext algorithm names from enabled and negotiated protocols; a request for `SSLContext.getInstance("TLS")` alone does not document which protocol versions are enabled or negotiated. Source: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html","Current Java SE 25 API documentation lists `TLSv1.2` and `TLSv1.3` among required SSLContext protocol algorithms, but support on older runtimes and non-default providers must be established from the relevant runtime/provider documentation. Oracle documents TLS 1.3 and the `TLSv1.3` SSLContext algorithm in JDK 11. Sources: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html ; https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/11-relnote-issues.html","The primary CrySL source scopes the specification to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`. Its event patterns name `getDefault`, `getInstance`, `init`, and `createSSLEngine`; the patterns express the relevant argument counts and bindings. The source’s matching and condition clauses are:

`SPEC javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`

`FORBIDDEN`
`	getDefault() => Get;`

`EVENTS`
`	g1: getInstance(protocol);`
`	g2: getInstance(protocol, _);`
`	Get := g1 | g2;`

`	i1: init(km, tm, random);`
`	Init := i1;`

`	se1: eng = createSSLEngine();`
`	se2: eng = createSSLEngine(_,_);`
`	Engine := se1 | se2;`

`ORDER`
`	Get, Init, Engine?`
`CONSTRAINTS`
`	protocol in {"TLSv1.2", "TLSv1.3"};`

`REQUIRES`
`	generatedKeyManagers[km];`
`	generatedTrustManagers[tm];`
`	randomized[random];`

Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl","Under that source text, the parameter-list patterns are: `getInstance(protocol)` and `getInstance(protocol, _)`; `init(km, tm, random)`; `createSSLEngine()` and `createSSLEngine(_,_)`; and forbidden `getDefault()`. The condition constrains the bound `protocol` to `"TLSv1.2"` or `"TLSv1.3"` and requires the three listed predicates for `km`, `tm`, and `random`. `Engine` is optional in `Get, Init, Engine?`. Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/CROSSINGTUD/Crypto-API-Rules/refs/heads/master/JavaCryptographicArchitecture/src/SSLContext.crysl","The rule source itself scopes its sole specification to `javax.net.ssl.SSLContext`; it declares no other receiver type. Accordingly, the source does not state that it matches a method merely because it shares one of the listed names on another type. The rule file does not document the detector’s dispatch-resolution implementation, so implementation-specific matching behavior beyond the declared `SPEC` scope is unresolved.
